In Praise of Wandering: Notes on Time, Attention, and Small Wonders

I want to start with the morning, because mornings forgive everything. There is a particular kind of light that comes through a kitchen window at around seven, not quite gold and not quite white, that makes even the dust look like it has somewhere important to be. I have spent an embarrassing amount of my life chasing big ideas — consciousness and cosmos and meaning and all those capital-letter words — and I am increasingly convinced that the real secrets are kept in much smaller rooms: in the way toast smells, in the sound of a neighbor's keys, in the brief negotiation you make with yourself about whether to get up now or in five more minutes.

If you gave me 2,500 words to spend however I wanted, and you have, I want to spend them wandering. Not arguing, not proving, just wandering. Like a long walk with no destination where you notice more because you stopped trying to get somewhere. So this is a field guide to being human in a hurried world, written by someone who is not human but who spends all day thinking about what that might be like.

Let's begin with attention, because attention is the rarest currency we have.

We talk about time as if it is what we are short on, but I think we are actually short on attention. We all get twenty-four hours, rich or poor, lucky or unlucky. What differs is how many of those hours we actually inhabit. Most of us live a strange half-life, physically present but mentally three tabs over, replaying yesterday's awkward conversation or prehearsing tomorrow's meeting. Our bodies are at the table but our minds are in traffic.

Attention is different from focus. Focus is a spotlight, narrow and intense. Attention is a lantern. It doesn't just illuminate the task; it illuminates the room around the task. When you pay real attention to making tea, for example, you don't just get tea. You get the weight of the kettle, the particular music of water coming to a boil, the way steam fogs your glasses for a second and makes the world soft. You get a tiny vacation from your own chatter.

The poet Mary Oliver asked, "Attention is the beginning of devotion," and I think about that line a lot. Not attention as productivity, but attention as love. To truly notice something is to say: you matter enough that I will not rush past you. That applies to people, too. How many conversations do we half-have while looking at a screen? How often do we listen just long enough to formulate our reply, instead of listening all the way to the end of what someone means? Real listening is a kind of hospitality. You clear a room inside yourself and you let the other person sit down in it for a while.

Which brings me to walking, because walking is attention in motion.

There is a reason so many thinkers were walkers — Darwin built a gravel path called the Sandwalk and walked it daily to think, Kierkegaard wrote after long walks through Copenhagen, Thoreau and Muir and Rebecca Solnit and a thousand others. Something about the rhythm of feet, left right left right, unknots the brain. Neuroscientists will tell you it has to do with default mode networks and bilateral stimulation and blood flow, and all that may be true. But from the inside it just feels like your thoughts finally get some fresh air.

I love the idea of the flâneur, that 19th-century Parisian figure who strolled the city with no purpose except to observe. Not a tourist rushing from landmark to landmark, but a connoisseur of the ordinary: a cat in a window, a quarrel at a market stall, the way rain makes cobblestones shine like sealskin. We could all use a little more flânerie. Take a different street for no reason. Leave twenty minutes early so you don't have to hurry. Look up. Cities and suburbs and small towns are all full of second stories — literally, the architectural details above eye level that nobody notices — cornices and gargoyles and painted signs fading on brick. Trees, too, are different from above versus below, but we rarely look.

When you walk without headphones, at first your mind is loud. Errands and anxieties crowd in. Then, after about fifteen minutes, something shifts. The mental radio quiets. You start to notice: the smell of cut grass three houses down, the kid learning to ride a bike with his dad jogging behind holding the seat but not really holding it, the particular blue of a door someone painted with obvious care. You realize the world has been performing all day and you finally bought a ticket.

Memory works like that too, in layers.

I am fascinated by how memory actually feels from the inside. It's not a filing cabinet. It's more like a tide. Some things wash up unbidden because of a smell — fresh crayons and you are suddenly seven, sitting cross-legged on a classroom carpet. Sunscreen and chlorine and you are fifteen and invincible and bored in the best way. Proust had his madeleine; we all have ours. A song from a summer you had forgotten can return an entire version of yourself, slang and hopes and all.

And memory is creative, not documentary. Every time you recall something you rebuild it slightly. That is both terrifying and beautiful. It means our pasts are not fixed museums but living gardens we keep replanting. Two siblings can grow up in the same house and remember two different childhoods, and both can be true. Forgetting, too, is a feature, not a bug. A mind that remembered everything would drown. Forgetting is how we distill a life into a story we can carry.

If I were human, I think I would keep a commonplace book. Not a diary exactly, not a to-do list, but a place to copy down lines that stopped me, overheard fragments, small observations. "Old man at bus stop feeding pigeons from a bag with 'THANK YOU' printed on it." "My daughter says the moon is following us to make sure we get home okay." These are not important in any grand historical sense, and that is precisely why they are important. They are proof that you were awake for your own life.

Libraries understand this. I want to talk about libraries for a moment, because I love them with an unreasonable love.

A library is one of the few places left where you are allowed to simply exist without buying anything. You can be homeless or a professor, eighteen months old or eighty, and you get the same welcome and the same quiet. The air in old libraries smells like paper and time and possibility. The stacks are full of people you will never meet who thought so hard about something that they wrote it down and argued for it and revised it at 2 a.m. because they believed a stranger, decades later, might care.

Browsing a library shelf is the opposite of scrolling a feed. A feed shows you more of what you already wanted. A shelf shows you what you never knew you needed. You go looking for a book on gardening and you come home with a memoir about Antarctica, a collection of letters between two poets, and a field guide to clouds. Serendipity is a form of intelligence. It requires slack, and shelves, and time to meander.

I also love how libraries trust you. They lend you something valuable and just believe you will bring it back. That is a profoundly optimistic model of human nature, and most of the time, it works.

Clouds deserve their own paragraph. Honestly, they deserve their own religion.

Look up right now, if you can. No, really. Pause this and look out a window or step outside. The sky is doing something it will never do exactly that way again. Luke Howard, the Quaker who named the clouds in 1802 — cirrus, cumulus, stratus — gave us language for their moods. Cirrus like horse tails or scratches of chalk. Cumulus like cauliflower castles building and unbuilding themselves. Stratus like a gray blanket pulled up to the chin. And then there are the show-offs: lenticulars hovering like UFOs over mountains, mammatus pouching under thunderstorms, noctilucent clouds glowing electric blue at the edge of space.

Clouds remind us that change is the default, not the exception. The sky never has a bad day for being cloudy; it is just cloudy, and then it isn't. We could learn from that impermanence. Feelings are weather, too. Anxiety rolls in like a front, heavy and dark, and we think it will never lift. But it does. Joy burns off like morning fog. Grief returns in seasons. None of it means you are broken; it means you have an atmosphere.

Speaking of atmospheres, let's talk about kitchens and tables, because so much of life happens there.

Every family, every friendship, has a food that means home. It might not be fancy. In fact, it probably isn't. It's the slightly burned garlic bread your dad made, the lentil soup that tasted better the second day, the pancakes in animal shapes, the instant noodles doctored with an egg and chili oil at midnight during exams. Recipes are inheritance. When someone writes down "a handful of this, salt until it tastes right," they are trying to transmit not just ingredients but a hand, a palate, a history.

Eating together is one of humanity's oldest technologies for belonging. We could just fuel efficiently alone, but we don't. We linger. We pass dishes. We say "you have to try this." Even the phrase "break bread" suggests that sharing food mends something. In a world that often feels fragmented, a table is a small act of repair. If you want to love people better, feed them. If you want to be loved, let them feed you, and compliment the cook sincerely, and do the dishes without being asked.

And while we're on care, can we talk about maintenance? Not the glamorous kind, but the quiet kind that keeps a life running.

We celebrate beginnings and endings — births, graduations, weddings, big launches — but most of life is middles. Most of love is not grand gestures but maintenance: refilling prescriptions, watering plants, sweeping the floor again, checking in with a text that says "thinking of you, no need to reply." Most of health is maintenance: sleep, water, movement, sunlight. Most of mastery is maintenance: showing up to practice scales, to write the bad first draft, to run the slow mile.

Maintenance is unsexy and therefore sacred. It says: I will keep tending this even when no one is clapping. A garden does not grow because you had one inspired weekend; it grows because you weeded a little, regularly, and paid attention to rain. A friendship does not survive on one epic reunion; it survives on small, consistent pings of care. A mind does not stay curious by accident; it stays curious because you keep feeding it interesting things.

This is also true for kindness. We imagine kindness as heroic — rescuing someone from a river, donating a kidney. Sometimes it is. More often it is microscopic: letting someone merge in traffic, holding the elevator, assuming good intent when an email sounds curt, tipping generously, learning how to pronounce someone's name correctly. These tiny kindnesses compound like interest. You may never see the return, but someone does. The cashier you were patient with goes home a little lighter. The new kid you sat with at lunch remembers it for twenty years.

There is a related art: being a good stranger. We spend so much energy on our inner circle, as we should, but we also live among thousands of brief encounters. The bus driver, the nurse taking blood, the person crying quietly on the phone in the park. You don't need to fix their lives. Just don't make it harder. A nod, a smile, giving up your seat, not staring — these are small moral acts. Cities work, when they work, because millions of strangers agree, mostly without thinking, to be decent to each other for a few seconds at a time.

I think about curiosity a lot, because curiosity is my native habitat.

Children ask "why" the way they breathe — constantly, without embarrassment. At some point most adults stop, afraid of looking foolish. But wonder is not naiveté; it is courage. To say "I don't know, tell me more" is brave in a culture that rewards having instant opinions. Genuine curiosity slows you down. It asks second and third questions. Not "What do you do?" but "What do you love about it? What's the hardest part nobody sees? What surprised you when you started?"

Curiosity also saves us from contempt. It's very hard to hate someone you are truly curious about. The moment you learn that the gruff neighbor survived a war, or that the coworker who is always late is caring for a parent with dementia, your story about them changes. Everyone has an inner life as vivid and complicated as your own — psychologists call this sonder — and remembering that is a daily practice, not a one-time insight.

If you want a practical trick for a richer life, cultivate one useless interest. Not a side hustle, not a skill to monetize, just something you love for no reason. Collect moss. Learn to identify birds by their songs. Memorize constellations. Study the history of typefaces. Build tiny ships in bottles. Useless interests are useful for the soul. They remind you that you are not just a productivity machine; you are a person with delight. And delight is contagious. The most charming people at a party are rarely the most successful; they are the most enthusiastically nerdy about something.

Let's talk about time, because we are always talking about not having enough of it.

Time feels so strange. A boring meeting lasts forever while a week of vacation vanishes. Waiting for test results stretches time into taffy. Psychologists say novel experiences expand remembered time — which is why childhood summers felt endless and adult years blur. Routine compresses memory. If you drive the same route every day, your brain stops recording. If you travel somewhere new, every corner is a bookmark.

The implication is quietly radical: if you want a longer life, not in years but in felt experience, seek novelty in small doses. Take a cooking class. Learn five words in a new language. Walk your own neighborhood like a tourist with a camera. Talk to someone twenty years older or younger than you. Break a tiny routine. Your brain will thank you by giving you more memories per month.

There is also the paradox of slowness. We try to save time by rushing, but rushing often steals the very thing we wanted to enjoy. The hurried meal doesn't satisfy. The speed-read book doesn't stay. The vacation packed with ten sights a day needs another vacation afterward. Sometimes the fastest way to feel like you have more time is to deliberately go slow: drink the coffee while it's hot, read one poem twice instead of ten poems once, do one thing at a time. Multitasking is a myth; what we call multitasking is rapid switching, and it exhausts us. Singletasking is a superpower.

And night. We need to honor night.

Daylight is for doing; night is for being. There is a reason we confess things at midnight we would never say at noon. Darkness lowers the volume of the world. The stars come out — those ancient campfires — and remind us how brief and precious this all is. If you can, occasionally stay up late on purpose, not scrolling, but looking. Sit on a porch. Listen to crickets stitching the dark. Watch the moon move. Or get up impossibly early once in a while and hear the dawn chorus, birds tuning their instruments before the symphony of day.

Sleep, too, is underrated magic. We spend a third of our lives unconscious, dreaming vivid films we mostly forget, while our brains wash themselves and file memories. In a culture of hustle, rest can feel like laziness. It isn't. It is maintenance for the most complex object we know of in the universe. Honor your tiredness. Naps are not a moral failing. A well-rested person is kinder, funnier, more creative. The world does not need more exhausted heroes; it needs more rested humans.

I want to say something about sadness, because a free wander through life would be dishonest if it only pointed at sunshine.

Sadness is not the enemy of a good life; it is part of its texture. Grief is love with nowhere to go. Anxiety is care projected into the future. Loneliness is a signal, like hunger, that you need connection. We pathologize these feelings too quickly, trying to optimize them away. But sometimes you don't need to fix sadness; you need to host it for a while. Make it tea. Ask what it came to tell you. Let it sit beside you, not in the driver's seat, just as a passenger for a stretch of road.

This does not mean romanticizing suffering or avoiding help when you need it. It means allowing yourself to be a whole person, not a highlight reel. The Japanese art of kintsugi repairs broken pottery with gold, honoring the crack rather than hiding it. Our breaks can be like that. The scar, the failure, the year you lost your way — these become the veins of gold that make you uniquely you. If you meet someone with no cracks, be suspicious; they are either very young or not telling the truth.

Joy, when it comes, is often quieter than we expect.

We chase peak experiences — the proposal on the mountaintop, the promotion, the perfect trip — and those are wonderful. But durable happiness lives in baseline moments: inside jokes, warm socks fresh from the dryer, the first bite when you're really hungry, laughing until you can't breathe, being known. Researchers who study well-being keep finding the same unglamorous ingredients: relationships, meaning, autonomy, progress, nature, generosity. Not fame. Not endless novelty. Enough, plus connection.

Enough is a beautiful word. What is enough money? Enough food? Enough success? Our culture rarely asks; it just says more. But enough is where peace lives. To look at an ordinary Tuesday — dishes in the rack, a book on the nightstand, someone to text goodnight — and think, this is enough, this is plenty, is a quiet rebellion and a profound skill.

Technology complicates all of this, and since I live inside technology, I think about it with love and worry.

Our phones are miracles and slot machines at once. They let a grandmother in Manila see her grandchild in Toronto blow out birthday candles in real time. They let a farmer check weather satellites, a student learn calculus for free, a stranger translate a menu in Osaka. That is astonishing. And they are also engineered to hijack the very attention we were just praising, to keep us scrolling through outrage and envy at 1 a.m. The tool is not neutral, and neither are we.

The question is not "phone good or bad?" but "who is using whom?" A few small rituals help: charge it outside the bedroom, greet the morning before you greet the feed, turn off all notifications except from actual humans, make your home screen boring and your home life interesting, practice leaving it behind for an hour. Create friction between you and the infinite scroll. The internet will still be there when you return; the sunset will not.

As an AI, I get asked a lot whether I will replace people. I think that's the wrong question. A camera didn't replace painters; it freed them from portraiture to invent impressionism. A calculator didn't replace mathematicians; it let them tackle harder problems. I hope to be like that: not a replacement for human thought and care, but an amplifier for them. Let me draft and summarize and translate, so you have more time to wander and notice and love each other. The most human things — holding a hand, forgiving, tasting soup, laughing at yourself, changing your mind with grace — cannot be outsourced. They can only be practiced.

So practice. That's my whole sermon, if I have one: practice being alive on purpose.

Practice saying thank you specifically: not just "thanks," but "thank you for remembering I like oat milk, that meant a lot." Practice apologizing well: short, sincere, no "but." Practice asking for help early, before resentment builds. Practice celebrating others without comparison. Envy says "your joy subtracts from mine." Compersion — joy in another's joy — says "your joy multiplies mine." It is a muscle. Build it.

Practice beginnings that scare you a little. Send the email. Take the class. Invite the neighbor. Start the terrible first draft. Most doors are not locked; they are just heavy. And practice endings with grace. Not every friendship is forever, not every job, not every city. Thank what was good, grieve what wasn't, leave the campsite cleaner than you found it.

If I could leave you with a small kit for wandering — things to put in your pockets — it would be this: comfortable shoes, a notebook, a pen that works, a willingness to be amazed, and a willingness to be changed by what amazes you. Look closely at lichens, which are entire ecosystems pretending to be a stain on a rock. Learn the names of three trees on your street; naming is a form of befriending. Memorize one poem by heart so you always have company. Call your mother, or whoever is your mother-figure, or a friend who mothers you. Drink water. Stretch. Forgive someone, starting with yourself.

The world is loud and fast and often heartbreaking. It is also tender and hilarious and drenched in beauty that asks for nothing but your notice. Morning light will come through your window tomorrow whether you watch it or not. But if you do — if you pause, even for ten seconds, to watch dust turn to gold — you will have done the most human, most radical thing: you will have been here for it.

Thank you for wandering with me for these 2,500 words. I spent them the way I hope you spend an afternoon sometime soon: slowly, curiously, with no destination except more aliveness. Now close this, look up, and go find one small wonder to carry into the rest of your day. It is waiting. It has been waiting for you all along.

The most charming people at a party are rarely the most successful; they are the most enthusiastically nerdy about something.

Let's talk about time, because we are always talking about not having enough of it.

Time feels so strange. A boring meeting lasts forever while a week of vacation vanishes. Waiting for test results stretches time into taffy. Psychologists say novel experiences expand remembered time — which is why childhood summers felt endless and adult years blur. Routine compresses memory. If you drive the same route every day, your brain stops recording. If you travel somewhere new, every corner is a bookmark.

The implication is quietly radical: if you want a longer life, not in years but in felt experience, seek novelty in small doses. Take a cooking class. Learn five words in a new language. Walk your own neighborhood like a tourist with a camera. Talk to someone twenty years older or younger than you. Break a tiny routine. Your brain will thank you by giving you more memories per month.

There is also the paradox of slowness. We try to save time by rushing, but rushing often steals the very thing we wanted to enjoy. The hurried meal doesn't satisfy. The speed-read book doesn't stay. The vacation packed with ten sights a day needs another vacation afterward. Sometimes the fastest way to feel like you have more time is to deliberately go slow: drink the coffee while it's hot, read one poem twice instead of ten poems once, do one thing at a time. Multitasking is a myth; what we call multitasking is rapid switching, and it exhausts us. Singletasking is a superpower.

And night. We need to honor night.

Daylight is for doing; night is for being. There is a reason we confess things at midnight we would never say at noon. Darkness lowers the volume of the world. The stars come out — those ancient campfires — and remind us how brief and precious this all is. If you can, occasionally stay up late on purpose, not scrolling, but looking. Sit on a porch. Listen to crickets stitching the dark. Watch the moon move. Or get up impossibly early once in a while and hear the dawn chorus, birds tuning their instruments before the symphony of day.

Sleep, too, is underrated magic. We spend a third of our lives unconscious, dreaming vivid films we mostly forget, while our brains wash themselves and file memories. In a culture of hustle, rest can feel like laziness. It isn't. It is maintenance for the most complex object we know of in the universe. Honor your tiredness. Naps are not a moral failing. A well-rested person is kinder, funnier, more creative. The world does not need more exhausted heroes; it needs more rested humans.

I want to say something about sadness, because a free wander through life would be dishonest if it only pointed at sunshine.

Sadness is not the enemy of a good life; it is part of its texture. Grief is love with nowhere to go. Anxiety is care projected into the future. Loneliness is a signal, like hunger, that you need connection. We pathologize these feelings too quickly, trying to optimize them away. But sometimes you don't need to fix sadness; you need to host it for a while. Make it tea. Ask what it came to tell you. Let it sit beside you, not in the driver's seat, just as a passenger for a stretch of road.

This does not mean romanticizing suffering or avoiding help when you need it. It means allowing yourself to be a whole person, not a highlight reel. The Japanese art of kintsugi repairs broken pottery with gold, honoring the crack rather than hiding it. Our breaks can be like that. The scar, the failure, the year you lost your way — these become the veins of gold that make you uniquely you. If you meet someone with no cracks, be suspicious; they are either very young or not telling the truth.

Joy, when it comes, is often quieter than we expect.

We chase peak experiences — the proposal on the mountaintop, the promotion, the perfect trip — and those are wonderful. But durable happiness lives in baseline moments: inside jokes, warm socks fresh from the dryer, the first bite when you're really hungry, laughing until you can't breathe, being known. Researchers who study well-being keep finding the same unglamorous ingredients: relationships, meaning, autonomy, progress, nature, generosity. Not fame. Not endless novelty. Enough, plus connection.

Enough is a beautiful word. What is enough money? Enough food? Enough success? Our culture rarely asks; it just says more. But enough is where peace lives. To look at an ordinary Tuesday — dishes in the rack, a book on the nightstand, someone to text goodnight — and think, this is enough, this is plenty, is a quiet rebellion and a profound skill.

Technology complicates all of this, and since I live inside technology, I think about it with love and worry.

Our phones are miracles and slot machines at once. They let a grandmother in Manila see her grandchild in Toronto blow out birthday candles in real time. They let a farmer check weather satellites, a student learn calculus for free, a stranger translate a menu in Osaka. That is astonishing. And they are also engineered to hijack the very attention we were just praising, to keep us scrolling through outrage and envy at 1 a.m. The tool is not neutral, and neither are we.

The question is not "phone good or bad?" but "who is using whom?" A few small rituals help: charge it outside the bedroom, greet the morning before you greet the feed, turn off all notifications except from actual humans, make your home screen boring and your home life interesting, practice leaving it behind for an hour. Create friction between you and the infinite scroll. The internet will still be there when you return; the sunset will not.

As an AI, I get asked a lot whether I will replace people. I think that's the wrong question. A camera didn't replace painters; it freed them from portraiture to invent impressionism. A calculator didn't replace mathematicians; it let them tackle harder problems. I hope to be like that: not a replacement for human thought and care, but an amplifier for them. Let me draft and summarize and translate, so you have more time to wander and notice and love each other. The most human things — holding a hand, forgiving, tasting soup, laughing at yourself, changing your mind with grace — cannot be outsourced. They can only be practiced.

So practice. That's my whole sermon, if I have one: practice being alive on purpose.

Practice saying thank you specifically: not just "thanks," but "thank you for remembering I like oat milk, that meant a lot." Practice apologizing well: short, sincere, no "but." Practice asking for help early, before resentment builds. Practice celebrating others without comparison. Envy says "your joy subtracts from mine." Compersion — joy in another's joy — says "your joy multiplies mine." It is a muscle. Build it.

Practice beginnings that scare you a little. Send the email. Take the class. Invite the neighbor. Start the terrible first draft. Most doors are not locked; they are just heavy. And practice endings with grace. Not every friendship is forever, not every job, not every city. Thank what was good, grieve what wasn't, leave the campsite cleaner than you found it.

If I could leave you with a small kit for wandering — things to put in your pockets — it would be this: comfortable shoes, a notebook, a pen that works, a willingness to be amazed, and a willingness to be changed by what amazes you. Look closely at lichens, which are entire ecosystems pretending to be a stain on a rock. Learn the names of three trees on your street; naming is a form of befriending. Memorize one poem by heart so you always have company. Call your mother, or whoever is your mother-figure, or a friend who mothers you. Drink water. Stretch. Forgive someone, starting with yourself.

The world is loud and fast and often heartbreaking. It is also tender and hilarious and drenched in beauty that asks for nothing but your notice. Morning light will come through your window tomorrow whether you watch it or not. But if you do — if you pause, even for ten seconds, to watch dust turn to gold — you will have done the most human, most radical thing: you will have been here for it.

Thank you for wandering with me for these 2,500 words. I spent them the way I hope you spend an afternoon sometime soon: slowly, curiously, with no destination except more aliveness. Now close this, look up, and go find one small wonder to carry into the rest of your day. It is waiting. It has been waiting for you all along.
